newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Welter of data to dominate.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Welter of data to dominate.

text.p: UK gilts face a hectic week, with a barrage of figures covering unemployment, earnings and retail prices due, and key data from the U.S. to keep an eye on too.

Gilts got off to a turbulent start to the week, with official statistics showing signs of a recovery in manufacturing, while a fresh bout of EMU uncertainty blew in from the Luxembourg Ecofin meeting of finance ministers.
"This is an important week for UK gilts. It's very difficult to say which way the market will bend ahead of all this data," CIBC chief economist David Coleman said.

A 0.6 percent jump in April manufacturing output, compared with a forecast 0.3 percent rise, knocked the stuffing out of gilt futures on Monday. The September contract was down 11/32 at 113-23 by 1300 GMT.
But Coleman said the lack of inflationary pressure evident meant the overall downside for gilts would be limited. Producer output prices prices rose just one percent year-on-year in May.

Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale, said Monday's data meant retail prices, due on Thursday and the week's key figure, should remain weak. "The figures show... manufacturers are able to increase output in the face of strong sterling. There is no reason to raise retail prices," he said.
Retail prices are forecast up 2.5 percent year-on-year in May, with the underlying rate at the same level, bang on the government's target.
Economists said tax not rate rises may be most effective in reining in the most buoyant parts of the British economy -- consumer spending and the service sector.
That leaves all eyes on Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2. But Friday's quarter-point interest rate rise probably did gilts no harm, they added.
"Friday's rate increase helped gilts. It suggests the Bank of England is not willing to take risks with inflation," Coleman said.

Wednesday's jobless data were likely to show unemployment remained on a sharp downtrend in May. A Reuter poll of economists forecast a further 40,000 drop in unemployment while average earnings growth was seen steady at an annual 4.5 percent in April.
Salomon Brothers' UK economist Michael Saunders said earnings would probably dip to around 4.25 percent in May as the effect of large City bonuses faded out.
That should mitigate against another rate rise soon as should Thursday's retail price data.
On the international scene, U.S. retail sales and producer price data are due on Thursday and Friday and are likely to reignite interest rate speculation over there, and hence worldwide.
But for the early part of the week, European economic and monetary union dominated again.

On Monday, new French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his EU counterparts that France was determined to see a single currency start in 1999 but that he wanted a period of reflection before signing the stability pact which sets out fines for countries not keeping their budget deficits in order.
That sparked immediate speculation about a delay for EMU or a fudging of the criteria. That should help gilts as Britain stands aloof from EMU, its opt-out intact.
"The UK, with its opt-out, is really standing aside from this," said Andrew Davies of London Bond Broking.

Although there was little sign of gilts gaining renewed safe haven status on Monday, as the strong manufacturing figures produced compensating fears of an overheating domestic economy, analysts said they should not underperform in any event.

The gilt/Bund spread stood at 144 basis points midway through Monday's session. It has hovered around 140 for the past few weeks having narrowed as far as 132 after Labour's storming election win on May 1.
But in absolute terms, gains could be hard to come by. Saunders at Salomon said gilts are already discounting a low inflation scenario.

"Yields are unlikely to drop below seven percent on a sustained basis unless the market can look forward to a period of falling base rates -- and that is unlikely in the near-term," he said. The benchmark 10-year gilt was yielding 7.09 percent on Monday.
